title: Trump’s AG Nominee Hangs in Balance as $1.8B Fund Flips from 'Dead' to Alive
summary: A political rollercoaster is unfolding in Washington. President Trump’s pick for Attorney General, Todd Blanche—his own former defense lawyer—faces a crucial Senate vote on Tuesday, but two Republican senators are digging in their heels. Sens. John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (North Carolina) refuse to support Blanche unless a $1.8 billion 'Anti-Weaponization Fund' is permanently scrapped. The fund, born from a lawsuit settlement, would compensate people who claim they were mistreated by the criminal justice system. It also controversially granted Trump and his family immunity from tax audits—a sticking point for the senators. On Friday, Trump declared the fund 'dead,' signaling a breakthrough. But by Saturday morning, he reversed course on Truth Social, threatening to keep Blanche as acting AG and 'push hard' to restore the fund if the senators don’t fall in line. He mocked both men for their electoral losses. Tillis shot back on X, accusing Trump of trying to 'resurrect the payout pot for punks' and warning that Blanche’s confirmation is now in jeopardy. Cornyn wants written guarantees that the tax-audit immunity is limited and retrospective. With the Judiciary Committee vote rescheduled for Tuesday, the White House is scrambling to secure votes before the August recess. The drama underscores Trump’s enduring loyalty to allies who feel persecuted—and his willingness to use leverage, even at the cost of his own nominee.
why_it_matters: The fight shows how loyalty and bargaining can delay the filling of the nation’s top law enforcement job, which affects everything from criminal trials to civil rights protections—making clear that politics often shapes who runs the justice system.

background_read: Todd Blanche was once a federal prosecutor before becoming one of Donald Trump’s personal defense lawyers in several criminal cases; now Trump wants him to run the entire Justice Department as Attorney General.
The Senate, where the vote will take place, has the constitutional power to confirm or reject a president’s cabinet picks—this is known as 'advice and consent'.

The Anti-Weaponization Fund came from a settlement in a lawsuit about the Trump Organization’s business practices; it included a controversial provision granting Trump and his family immunity from tax audits.
When the Senate is in session, its Judiciary Committee reviews legal nominees and sends a recommendation to the full Senate; delays can mean the position remains unfilled.
The August recess is a long break that Congress takes each summer; if a vote does not happen before then, Blanche may stay as acting AG indefinitely.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A political rollercoaster surrounds Trump's AG pick.
└─ HOOK: Two Republican senators are digging in their heels.
KEY EVENT: Sens. Cornyn and Tillis oppose Blanche over the $1.8 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund.
├─ WHO: Todd Blanche (ex-defense lawyer, nominee), Sens. John Cornyn (Texas) & Thom Tillis (North Carolina).
├─ WHAT: Fund grants immunity from tax audits; senators demand it be scrapped; Cornyn wants written guarantee of limited, retrospective immunity.
├─ WHEN: Friday (Trump declares fund dead) → Saturday (reverses on Truth Social, mocks senators).
└─ CONSEQUENCE: Trump threatens to keep Blanche as acting AG and restore the fund if senators resist.
├─ TRUMP’S STANCE: Uses fund as leverage; says senators must fall in line; mocks their election losses.
└─ SENATORS’ STANCE: Tillis accuses Trump of resurrecting a 'payout pot for punks'; warns confirmation is in jeopardy.
OPEN QUESTION: Can the White House secure enough votes before Tuesday’s committee vote and the August recess?

perspectives.description: Backers argue that the fund compensates people who are wrongly treated by prosecutors or police, deterring misconduct. They see it as a needed check on power, even if critics call it a giveaway to Trump associates.

Opponents view the fund as a slush fund that shields the powerful from accountability, especially the tax-audit immunity. Sens. Cornyn and Tillis believe it rewards wrongdoing and undermines public trust in equal justice.

The standoff is a classic test of checks and balances: the Senate’s confirmation power vs. a president’s desire to protect allies. It mirrors past fights where nominees became bargaining chips, and it reveals how a single provision can derail major appointments.

If Blanche remains acting AG indefinitely without a vote, the Senate’s confirmation role might weaken. Conversely, a compromise on the fund could set a precedent for limiting self-serving legal protections, but the fund’s future—and Blanche’s status—will likely stay unsettled until the August recess deadline.
